arXiv:2605.13687v1 [cs.LG] 13 May 2026

A Hierarchical Language Model with Predictable Scaling Laws and Provable Benefits of Reasoning

Jason Gaitonde Affiliation: Duke University    Frederic Koehler Affiliation: University of Chicago    Elchanan Mossel Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology    Joonhyung Shin Affiliation: University of Chicago    Allan Sly Affiliation: Princeton University
Abstract

We introduce a family of synthetic languages with hierarchical structure — generated by a broadcast process on trees — for which the role of context length and reasoning in autoregressive generation can be analyzed precisely. At the heart of our analytic approach is an exact kk-gram ansatz in place of transformers with context length kk, a substitution we then validate empirically. Using this ansatz we derive explicit asymptotic predictions for distributional statistics of the sequences produced by a trained model, instantiated in two settings. For the Ising broadcast process (a soft-constrained language), we prove that the variance of the generated sum scales log-linearly in the context depth and its kurtosis converges to that of a Gaussian — both deviating from the true language for any sublinear context. For the coloring broadcast process (a hard-constrained language) in the freezing regime, bounded-context autoregression produces sequences that, with high probability, are inconsistent with any valid coloring of the underlying tree. Together these results imply an Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) lower bound on the context length required to faithfully sample length-nn sequences. In contrast, we prove that an autoregressive reasoning model with only Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) working memory can sample exactly from the true language — an exponential improvement. We confirm both the lower-bound predictions and the reasoning-based upper bound empirically with transformers trained on the synthetic language; the trained models track our asymptotic predictions quantitatively across a wide range of context sizes.

1 Introduction

The size of an autoregressive language model’s context window is one of the central design parameters in modern LLMs. Larger contexts allow more long-range dependencies to be captured (Vaswani et al., 2017), are essential for the reasoning/chain-of-thought paradigm (Xiong et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Jaech et al., 2024), and empirically obey scaling laws relating context size to predictive loss (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). They are also expensive: the quadratic cost of attention in the context length has driven substantial research into scaling contexts up (Dao et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2025; Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). Despite this centrality, a sharp theoretical understanding of what context length buys — and when reasoning can substitute for it — has remained elusive. A core obstacle is the difficulty of formulating quantitative distributional questions about generated text when the underlying language distribution is unknown.

A hierarchical language with tractable statistics.

In this work we study a class of synthetic languages for which the underlying distribution is both known exactly and admits a clean asymptotic analysis. The language is generated by a broadcast process on a dd-ary tree: a root token is sampled from a prior and then propagated downward through a noisy channel until it reaches the dhd^{h} leaves, which form the observed sequence. Variants of this model have a long history in probability and statistical physics, and have recently been used as a substrate for theoretical questions about deep learning (Mossel, 2016; Cagnetta et al., 2024; Tomasini and Wyart, 2024; Ren et al., 2026). Crucially, the model is not merely a “formal language” (i.e., a set of valid strings) but a probability distribution over strings, which is what generative pretraining actually targets via maximum likelihood. The hierarchical structure also reflects a long tradition in linguistics and NLP that treats language as compositional and multiscale (Chomsky, 1957; Jurafsky and Martin, 2026; Elman, 1990; Ebeling and Neiman, 1995; Yang et al., 2016): parse trees, semantic dependencies, and discourse structure all impose correlations across widely separated length scales.

We emphasize that tree-structured representations of language are ubiquitous. Hierarchical sentence diagrams appear in 19th-century pedagogical grammars (Reed and Kellogg, 1877), and immediate constituent analysis (Bloomfield, 1933; Wells, 1947) formalized the view that sentences decompose recursively into nested constituents. Chomsky (1957) and Tesnière (1959) both represented sentences using hierarchical tree structures, and compositional semantics assigns meaning to a sentence by recursively combining the meanings of its subtrees (Montague, 1970). NLP inherited this perspective, from probabilistic context-free grammars (Jurafsky and Martin, 2026) and treebank-based parsing (Marcus et al., 1993) to tree-structured neural networks (Socher et al., 2013; Tai et al., 2015). The broadcast model can be viewed as a probabilistic generative process on such a tree, with the latent internal nodes playing the role of unobserved syntactic or semantic structure.

The broadcast model on trees.

Let Td,hT_{d,h} denote the dd-ary tree of height hh, and let Σ\Sigma be a finite set of tokens. The (d,h,κ,ν)(d,h,\kappa,\nu)-broadcast process samples a token at each node of the tree as follows: the root is drawn from a prior ν\nu over Σ\Sigma, and each non-root node, given the value at its parent, is sampled independently according to a transition kernel κ\kappa on Σ\Sigma. The language is defined as the joint distribution over the dhd^{h} leaf tokens, viewed as a distribution on Σdh\Sigma^{d^{h}}. See Section 2 for full details.

In this paper we focus on two instantiations of this model: the Ising broadcast process, where Σ={±1}\Sigma=\{\pm 1\} and κ\kappa copies the parent with probability ρ\rho and re-randomizes otherwise, modeling soft global correlations; and the coloring broadcast process, where Σ=[q]\Sigma=[q] and κ\kappa samples a uniformly random color for each child which differs from its parent. The latter models hard logical constraints analogous to those in code or formal mathematics. In either case, internal nodes can be interpreted as latent high-level topics or syntactic structure that constrains the observed tokens at the leaves.

For our experiments, the leaf sequence is tokenized with hierarchical punctuation marks delimiting subtrees at each level — analogous to how natural language uses commas, periods, and paragraph breaks to mark structure at different scales — so that a bounded-context model can locate itself within the hierarchy. See Section 4 for details. Our theoretical results, which concern the marginal distribution over leaf values, are unaffected by this tokenization choice.

Our analysis: quantitative predictions for trained transformers via a kk-gram ansatz.

Our key technical idea is to analyze, in place of a transformer with context length kk, the optimal autoregressive process that depends only on the previous kk tokens. We refer to this as the kk-gram ansatz. While kk-gram models with large kk are well known to be statistically and computationally intractable in general (Shannon, 1948; Jurafsky and Martin, 2026), in our hierarchical model the distribution of kk-gram is tractable, and we use it to derive explicit scaling laws for distributional statistics of the generated sequence. We then show experimentally that transformers trained on the same synthetic language closely match these predictions: the variance, kurtosis, and validity-rate curves of the trained models track our asymptotic theory across a wide range of context sizes.

1.1 Summary of our results

We now describe our main theoretical contributions, which fall into two parts: lower bounds showing that bounded-context autoregression is observably inconsistent with the true language, and an upper bound showing that logarithmic-memory reasoning suffices to generate from it exactly.

Lower bounds: scaling laws and Gaussianity for Ising.

Our lower bounds concern an autoregressive variant of the broadcast process (Definition 2.2) in which each subtree of size dwd^{w} is generated using only the previous dwd^{w} tokens. For the Ising broadcast process above the Kesten–Stigum threshold d​ρ2>1d\rho^{2}>1, we prove that the normalized variance of the generated sum of tokens scales log-linearly in the context depth ww, and that its kurtosis converges to that of a Gaussian (3.1 and 3.2). Both effects imply that the global coherence of the generated language is polynomially smaller than that of the true language unless ww is within O⁡(1)O(1) of hh, and both are matched quantitatively by transformers trained on the synthetic language (Figure 1).

Lower bounds: inconsistent generation for coloring.

For the coloring broadcast process in the freezing regime — where the branching factor dd is sufficiently large compared to the number of colors qq — we prove that any bounded-context autoregressive model produces, with high probability, sequences that are inconsistent with any proper coloring of Td,hT_{d,h} (Theorem 3.3). This is a qualitatively different failure mode from the Ising case: not statistical decoherence but outright invalidity, analogous to code in which individual functions compile but the program as a whole does not. We confirm this prediction empirically (Figure 2).

Upper bound: logarithmic reasoning suffices.

In contrast to these lower bounds, we prove that an autoregressive reasoning model — one equipped with a working memory of O⁡(h​log⁡d)=O⁡(log⁡n)O(h\log d)=O(\log n) bits that can be read from and written to during generation — can sample exactly from the true (d,h,κ,ν)(d,h,\kappa,\nu)-language (Theorem 3.4). This is an exponential improvement over what is achievable without reasoning: our lower bounds show that any non-reasoning model needs Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) context to even approximately match simple global statistics, while Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) reasoning bits suffice to sample exactly. Trained transformers equipped with reasoning traces match the true language empirically across all our settings, with context windows orders of magnitude smaller than the language length.

1.2 Related Work

Hierarchical language models.

A fundamental question in the theory of deep learning is understanding why depth is necessary, that is, identifying natural data distributions for which deep architectures provably outperform shallow ones. Mossel (2016) proposed to study hierarchical generative models based on broadcast on trees with the goal of representing data such as images or languages. Mossel observed that efficient algorithms for reconstructing such models follow from known results on phylogenetic reconstruction and established a separation in the semi-supervised setting below the Kesten-Stigum bound. Follow up results established low-degree hardness in the same regime (Koehler and Mossel, 2022; Huang and Mossel, 2024; Huang and Mossel, 2025). More recent work in physics (Cagnetta et al., 2024; Tomasini and Wyart, 2024) analyzed variants of this model and demonstrate that both gradient descent and diffusion-based methods experimentally learn their model in the easy regime (i.e. above the Kesten-Stigum bound). Ren et al. (2026) prove that, under mild conditions, a deep convolutional network with gradient descent-based methods and layerwise training can efficiently learn this class.

Formal languages and the representational power of transformers.

A number of recent works have studied the representational power of the transformer architecture from the perspective of formal languages and worst-case complexity theory. See, e.g., Pérez et al. (2021); Barceló et al. (2023); Chiang et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2025); Merrill and Sabharwal (2023b). For example, Merrill and Sabharwal (2023b) showed that log-precision transformers are contained within the class T​C0TC^{0} of bounded-depth circuits, while Pérez et al. (2021); Merrill and Sabharwal (2023a); Feng et al. (2023) show that transformers with the ability to generate intermediate states, i.e. with reasoning/CoT, are Turing complete. So from the perspective of worst-case complexity theory (and assuming standard conjectures, c.f., Chen et al. (2025)), reasoning/CoT are known to be crucial to allow transformers to represent many languages. In fact, once CoT is introduced, even relatively simple models like linear next-token-predictors become Turing complete (Malach, 2023).

The aforementioned results are largely existential, i.e., investigate the representational ability of transformers. However, existence alone does not imply that standard training methods, or indeed that any method, can efficiently learn such a model from examples. Conjecturally hard examples like the problem of learning sparse parities with noise (Blum et al., 2003) show that learning even quite easy-to-represent concepts from data can be cryptographically hard (see related discussion in Malach (2023)). In contrast, for the hierarchical languages we study, we can experimentally demonstrate that the behavior of realistic transformer architectures, trained via next-token-prediction in the usual way, exhibits close agreement with our theoretical predictions.

Learning-theoretic perspectives on reasoning/CoT.

The recent works of Malach (2023); Joshi et al. (2025) study the effect of CoT on the computational and statistical tractability of learning. One important finding is that the inclusion of short reasoning traces (of O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) length for an input of length nn) in the training data can allow autoregressive models to learn functions like parities with noise which are cryptographically hard when the reasoning traces are omitted. The benefit of reasoning in our model is similar, in that a O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) length reasoning trace enables learning both theoretically and experimentally, but the underlying mechanism is statistical rather than computational. Without the reasoning trace, we show that the transformer with sublinear context windows progressively loses information about the past, which causes it to incorrectly generate the language. This in turn is driven by the hierarchical structure of our language, where information naturally flows over different length scales, which is absent from constructions like sparse parities.

Other related work.

As discussed in the introduction, the computational challenge caused by the quadratic time-complexity of the attention mechanism, and the importance of being able to attend to large contexts, are considered to be extremely important considerations in the design and use of SoTA language models. Our reasoning example partially fits into the paradigm of context compression/compaction. See Anthropic (2025) for discussion of the fundamental importance of context management in Claude Code and other applications.

Our kk-gram ansatz is partially motivated by a theoretical work of Sharan et al. (2018), which showed some positive results for modeling languages with bounded mutual information over large length scales using simple kk-gram models. Practical kk-gram models are restricted to relatively short contexts since their state space grows exponentially with the length of their memory; however, we might hope that transformers with sublinear windows on natural languages may be able to learn good approximations to the corresponding (intractible) kk-gram model. As a reminder, kk-gram models themselves date back to the early mathematical studies of natural language by Shannon (1948) — see, e.g., Jurafsky and Martin (2026) for more background.

1.3 Organization

In Section 2 we define the ground truth generative model in full detail. In Section 3 we formally state our main theoretical results, leaving the detailed proofs to the appendices. In Section 4 we confirm our theoretical predictions with experiments on transformers trained on the synthetic language.

2 Broadcast Process as a Hierarchical Language Model

Formally, our hierarchical model of language follows the “broadcast process on trees":

Definition 2.1 (Broadcast Model).

Let Td,hT_{d,h} denote the dd-ary tree of depth hh and let Σ\Sigma denote a finite set of tokens. We index the non-root nodes of Td,hT_{d,h} by writing a node rr at level ℓ\ell as r∈[d]ℓr\in[d]^{\ell}. Given a probability transition kernel κ\kappa on Σ\Sigma — called the broadcast channel — and the initial prior ν\nu on the root, the (d,h,κ,ν)(d,h,\kappa,\nu)-broadcast process on Td,hT_{d,h} is generated as follows:

  1. 1.

    Sample the root value X∅∼νX_{\emptyset}\sim\nu.

  2. 2.

    Given the values at a layer ℓ≤h−1\ell\leq h-1, independently sample XrX_{r} for r∈[d]ℓ+1r\in[d]^{\ell+1} according to the law

    μr(σ)=κ(Xr[1:ℓ],σ),σ∈Σ.\mu_{r}(\sigma)=\kappa(X_{r[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\ell]},\sigma)\,,\qquad\sigma\in\Sigma\,.

We write XL∈ΣdhX_{L}\in\Sigma^{d^{h}} for the sequence of tokens at the leaves. The (d,h,κ,ν)(d,h,\kappa,\nu)-language is defined by the law of XLX_{L}, which is a distribution on Σdh\Sigma^{d^{h}}. When ν\nu is omitted, it is the stationary distribution.

We will study two particular broadcast processes: first, the Ising broadcast process is defined by the state space Σ={−1,+1}\Sigma=\{-1,+1\} and the broadcast channel

κ⁡(σ,σ′)={1+ρ2if σ=σ′,1−ρ2otherwise\kappa(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})=\begin{cases}\frac{1+\rho}{2}&\text{if $\sigma=\sigma^{\prime}$,}\\ \frac{1-\rho}{2}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

for a correlation parameter ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1], and the Rademacher prior ν\nu. In particular, a child copies its parent’s state with probability ρ\rho and re-randomizes with probability 1−ρ1-\rho. We also consider the coloring broadcast process with state space Σ=[q]\Sigma=[q] and broadcast channel

κ⁡(σ,σ′)={0if σ=σ′,1q−1otherwise\kappa(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $\sigma=\sigma^{\prime}$,}\\ \frac{1}{q-1}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

for a fixed constant q≥2q\geq 2 representing the number of colors, and the uniform prior ν\nu on Σ\Sigma. Here, a child randomly picks a color not chosen by its parent. This process was studied extensively in probability and statistical physics starting with Kesten and Stigum (1966b); Higuchi (1977); Spitzer (1975), further background can be found in Evans et al. (2000); Mossel (2004); Mézard and Montanari (2006); Mossel (2022).

Our main theoretical results will compare the statistics of the broadcast process with a Markovian version that has sublinear length to generate new subtrees:

Definition 2.2 (Autoregressive Broadcast Process).

Given parameters d,h,κd,h,\kappa as in Definition 2.1, the (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-autoregressive broadcast process with context depth w≤hw\leq h is the stochastic process XL∈ΣdhX^{L}\in\Sigma^{d^{h}} generated as follows:

  1. 1.

    Sample Y1∈ΣdwY_{1}\in\Sigma^{d^{w}} from the marginal of the (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-broadcast process on (any) subtree of size dwd^{w}.

  2. 2.

    For r=2,…,dh−wr=2,\ldots,d^{h-w}, sample YrY_{r} by sampling first hr∈{1,…,h−w}h_{r}\in\{1,\ldots,h-w\} independently from the distribution of heights between subtrees of depth ww in Td,hT_{d,h} and then sampling YrY_{r} from the (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-broadcast process conditioned on Yr−1Y_{r-1} and with these subtrees having least common ancestor in Td,hT_{d,h} at height exactly hrh_{r}.

The final sample is XL=(Y1,…,Ydh−w)∈ΣdhX_{L}=(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{d^{h-w}})\in\Sigma^{d^{h}}.

The autoregressive broadcast produces a sample XLX_{L} by sampling on subtrees of Td,hT_{d,h} of size dwd^{w} one at a time. In each generation step, the autoregressive process conditions just on the previous subtree to produce the next subtree. The conditional distribution of this next subtree is simulated from the original broadcast process by averaging over the conditional distribution of adjacent subtrees in the original process, taken over the random height of the least common ancestor which governs the signal between these subtrees. In other words, the generation step samples adjacent subtrees according to the law of the broadcast process for a random pair of adjacent subtrees in Td,hT_{d,h}.

Note that this process is slightly different from the vanilla token-by-token auto-regressive process, because it is more mathematically elegant to analyze a process where you generate one depth ww sub-tree at a time. We expect the same results hold for generating one token at a time (which is how we run the experiments), at the cost of a more complicated proof.

3 Theoretical results

Our main technical results concern the power of autoregressive models where they are only allowed to regress on the limited number of the most recent outputs. We consider models that, given an empty prompt or the leaves of a dd-ary tree with height ww, output the leaves of a (random) dd-ary tree with height ww, where ww is the context depth as in Definition 2.2. This corresponds to a transition kernel (conditional distribution function)

p(⋅∣−):Σdw∪{∅}→𝒫(Σdw)p(\cdot\mid-)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\Sigma^{d^{w}}\cup\{\emptyset\}\to\mathcal{P}(\Sigma^{d^{w}})

where 𝒫⁡(Σdw)\mathcal{P}(\Sigma^{d^{w}}) is the set of probability measures on Σdw\Sigma^{d^{w}}; this is equivalent to considering models with Θ⁡(dw​log⁡|Σ|)\Theta(d^{w}\log|\Sigma|) bits of context. Running this model dh−wd^{h-w} times autoregressively, starting with the initial prompt ∅\emptyset, samples a sequence in Σdh\Sigma^{d^{h}}, and our goal is to compare the distribution of this generated sequence to the ground truth (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-language.

For simple autoregressive models without reasoning, we consider that the generative model is trained on data generated in the following way:

  1. 1.

    Sample a (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-language XLX_{L} of Td,hT_{d,h}.

  2. 2.

    Sample a subtree index ii uniformly at random from [dh−w]={1,2,⋯,dh−w}[d^{h-w}]=\{1,2,\cdots,d^{h-w}\}.

  3. 3.

    If i≥2i\geq 2, then the input is the leaves Yi−1Y_{i-1} of the (i−1)(i-1)th subtree of Td,hT_{d,h}, and the output is the leaves YiY_{i} of the iith subtree of Td,hT_{d,h}. If i=1i=1, then the input is an empty prompt.

Since the model can only look at the subtree of height ww each step, this is equivalent to training on the (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-autoregressive broadcast process, and the optimal model will exactly generate the (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-autoregressive broadcast process. Thus, it suffices to compare the full broadcast process (Definition 2.1) to its Markovian autoregressive variant (Definition 2.2).

A natural question is how the global statistics of the autoregressively generated sequence scale with the context length ww as the language length dhd^{h} grows. This section answers this question for the Ising and coloring broadcast processes (Sections 3.1 and 3.2), and shows that an exponentially smaller amount of reasoning memory suffices to recover the true distribution exactly (Section 3.3).

Appendices.

Proofs of theorems for Section 3.1 are deferred to Appendix D, for Section 3.2 to Appendix E, and for Section 3.3 to Appendix F.

3.1 Ising Broadcast Process

For the Ising broadcast process, a natural statistic is the variance of the sum of tokens normalized by dh/2d^{h/2}, which measures the global alignment of the language. For the true (non-autoregressive) language, the sum of tokens is well-understood: above the Kesten–Stigum threshold d​ρ2>1d\rho^{2}>1, this statistic becomes correlated with the latent root token even as h→∞h\to\infty (Kesten and Stigum, 1966a), see also Janson and Mossel (2004), and the normalized variance becomes exponentially large in the height hh (see (2)). The following theorem shows that the autoregressive variant exhibits a sharply different behavior in this regime.

Theorem 3.1.

Consider the Ising broadcast process on Td,hT_{d,h} with d​ρ2>1d\rho^{2}>1. For a given context depth 0≤w≤h0\leq w\leq h, let XL∈{±1}dhX_{L}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d^{h}} denote a sample from the autoregressive process on the leaves with context length dwd^{w}. Then if w→∞w\to\infty and h−w→∞h-w\to\infty, the (log-) normalized variance satisfies:

log⁡(d−h⋅𝖵𝖺𝗋⁡(∑i=1dh(XL)i))=w​log⁡(d​ρ2)+log⁡(Ad,ρ​(2))+o⁡(1),\log\left(d^{-h}\cdot\mathsf{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d^{h}}(X_{L})_{i}\right)\right)=w\log(d\rho^{2})+\log(A_{d,\rho}(2))+o(1), (1)

where Ad,ρ​(2)A_{d,\rho}(2) is an explicit constant depending only on d,ρd,\rho.

By contrast, when XL∈{±1}dhX_{L}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d^{h}} is a sample from the true Ising broadcast process (i.e. w=hw=h),

log⁡(d−h⋅𝖵𝖺𝗋⁡(∑i=1dh(XL)i))=h​log⁡(d​ρ2)+log⁡(Cd,ρ​(2))+o⁡(1),\log\left(d^{-h}\cdot\mathsf{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d^{h}}(X_{L})_{i}\right)\right)=h\log(d\rho^{2})+\log(C_{d,\rho}(2))+o(1), (2)

where Cd,ρ​(2)≤Ad,ρ​(2)C_{d,\rho}(2)\leq A_{d,\rho}(2) is an explicit constant depending only on d,ρd,\rho.11 1 The different constant terms reflect that when ww is very close to hh, there are finite-size corrections to the asymptotics.

Theorem 3.1 has two implications. First, while the autoregressive process produces tokens with the correct local marginals by definition, its global coherence is polynomially smaller than the true language’s unless a linear fraction of the language is used as context (w=h−O⁡(1)w=h-O(1)). In the context of natural language, this can be thought of as failing to produce a strong unified signal — for example, generating a long, ambiguous answer to a yes/no question rather than committing to a direction. Second, the prediction is precisely quantitative: the log-variance is linear in ww with slope log⁡(d​ρ2)\log(d\rho^{2}), which our experiments on trained transformers confirm closely (Figure 1(a)).

This decoherence has a further observable consequence. By computing higher moments of the autoregressive process via the theory of broadcast processes, we obtain the following result:

Theorem 3.2.

Consider the Ising broadcast process on Td,hT_{d,h} with d​ρ2>1d\rho^{2}>1. For a given context depth 0≤w≤h0\leq w\leq h, let XL∈{±1}dhX_{L}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d^{h}} denote a sample from the autoregressive process on the leaves with context length dwd^{w}. If w→∞w\to\infty and h−w→∞h-w\to\infty, then the excess kurtosis of ∑i(XL)i\sum_{i}(X_{L})_{i} satisfies:

Kurt⁡(∑i=1dh(XL)i)−3:=𝔼⁡[(∑i=1dh(XL)i)4]𝔼​[(∑i=1dh(XL)i)2]2−3=o⁡(1).\mathrm{Kurt}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d^{h}}(X_{L})_{i}\right)-3\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d^{h}}(X_{L})_{i}\right)^{4}\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d^{h}}(X_{L})_{i}\right)^{2}\right]^{2}}-3=o(1)\,. (3)

Recall that the kurtosis of Gaussian random variables is precisely 33. Intuitively, Theorem 3.2 says that bounded-context autoregression in this hierarchical language causes information decay rapid enough for central-limit-type behavior to emerge: the generated sum behaves like a sum of approximately independent contributions from each subtree, even though the true language has heavy-tailed multiscale dependencies.Our experiments again confirm this prediction (Figure 1(b)).

3.2 Coloring Broadcast Process

The previous results quantify the behavior of bounded-context autoregression in a soft-constrained language: every sequence has positive probability under the true language, and the generated sequences differ from it statistically rather than logically. Many real applications of language models involve hard-constrained languages, where logical or syntactic rules exclude entire classes of sequences — code, formal mathematics, structured data, and so on. The coloring broadcast process serves as a clean abstraction of this setting: by construction, valid sequences correspond exactly to leaf labelings extending to a proper coloring of the underlying tree.

A central phenomenon in the theory of colorings on trees is freezing (e.g. Mossel and Peres (2003); Semerjian (2008); Sly (2009)): when dd is sufficiently large relative to qq, the leaves of a subtree contain enough information to typically fix all of the internal labels, including the root. We demonstrate that freezing has stark consequences for autoregressive generation.

Theorem 3.3.

Consider the autoregressive coloring broadcast process with qq colors on Td,hT_{d,h} with any context depth w<hw<h satisfying d>q⁡(log⁡(q)+log⁡log⁡(q)+1+oq​(1))d>q(\log(q)+\log\log(q)+1+o_{q}(1)). Then with probability 1−oq​(1)1-o_{q}(1), the sampling of the leaves in the autoregressive coloring process is inconsistent with any proper coloring of Td,hT_{d,h}.

The interpretation is that with bounded context, the autoregressive process samples each subtree consistently with itself but cannot maintain global consistency across subtrees, as freezing-determined “commitments” made at the leaves of one subtree generically conflict with those of another. In the natural-language analogy: each subtree corresponds to a coherent local fragment, but the overall sequence has no globally valid parse. The empirical counterpart in Figure 2 shows that trained transformers in this regime almost never produce a valid sequence, while reasoning-equipped models almost always do.

3.3 Autoregressive Models with Reasoning

We model a reasoning-equipped autoregressive model as the ordinary autoregressive model augmented with an additional working memory — a finite set ℳ\mathcal{M} of memory states that the model may freely read from or write to between generation steps, and whose contents are not part of the final output. The model is then a transition kernel (conditional distribution function)

p(⋅∣−):(Σdw∪{∅})×ℳ→𝒫(Σdw×ℳ).p(\cdot\mid-)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}(\Sigma^{d^{w}}\cup\{\emptyset\})\times\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{P}(\Sigma^{d^{w}}\times\mathcal{M})\,. (4)

The size of the memory log⁡|ℳ|\log|\mathcal{M}| is the relevant “reasoning budget,” analogous to the length of a chain-of-thought trace in real LLMs. The next theorem shows that a logarithmic budget is sufficient to sample the true language exactly, even with arbitrarily small context.

Theorem 3.4.

For any 0≤w≤h0\leq w\leq h, |ℳ|=(d​|Σ|)O⁡(h−w)|\mathcal{M}|=(d|\Sigma|)^{O(h-w)} suffices to sample from the exact (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-language. In particular, there is an autoregressive reasoning model with context size O⁡(h​log⁡(d​|Σ|))O(h\log(d|\Sigma|)) that samples from the ground truth language (when w=0w=0 is chosen).

This result is agnostic to the broadcast channel κ\kappa. The intuition is that the memory only needs to carry information about the path from the root to the current generation position in the tree — specifically, the labels of the O⁡(h)O(h) ancestors and recent siblings needed to sample the next subtree from the true conditional distribution. This is O⁡(h​log⁡d​|Σ|)=O⁡(log⁡n)O(h\log d|\Sigma|)=O(\log n) bits of state, exponentially smaller than the Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) context required by a non-reasoning model. Connecting back to practice, this offers a clean theoretical analogue to the context-compression phenomenon studied in modern LLMs (Anthropic, 2025): a small, well-chosen working memory can substitute for a much larger context window, provided the underlying distribution has compressible hierarchical structure.

4 Empirical Results

We corroborate our theory by empirically demonstrating the scaling law for the two broadcast processes: the sum of leaves for the Ising model, and the success rate of root reconstruction for the coloring model. We use nanochat by Karpathy (2025) as our base model and train on the dataset synthetically generated from our hierarchical language described in Section 2. Then we evaluate the empirical distribution of the output generated by the autoregressive sampling of the pre-trained model. Our codes for experiments are available in https://github.com/joonhyungshin/nanocontext. See Appendix G for the detailed experiment setup.

Punctuation.

A notable detail in the tokenization step of our language is the introduction of punctuation marks. Recall that our hierarchical language is a sequence of the dhd^{h} leaves of a dd-ary tree with height hh, with latent internal nodes that affect the leaves in its subtree. We insert a punctuation mark every dd values in the sequence, effectively telling the model that “a certain subtree has concluded, and a new subtree begins.” We use different punctuation tokens for different height of the subtrees, analogous to natural language documents which have different indicators at different levels (commas, periods, line breaks, etc.). Including the punctuation marks, we use dh−1​(d+1)−1d^{h-1}(d+1)-1 many tokens to tokenize a dd-ary tree with height hh. See Figure 3 for an illustrative example.

Autoregressive training.

Recall that in our theoretical results in Section 3, we considered restrictive models that samples a subtree given the previous subtree. To evaluate under a more practical scenario, we do not follow this restriction in our experiments. Instead, we do the usual autoregressive training: the training samples are “chunks” CC of the leaves of length kk equal to the prescribed context size, and train the model to predict C[2:k+1]C[2\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}k+1] given C[1:k]C[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}k]. During the inference, the model autoregressively outputs a token one at a time, where the current output is fed back as the most recent token of the input and the oldest token is truncated in case the number of tokens exceeds kk. Here, the punctuation marks described in the previous paragraph play a vital role, since it tells the model what part of the subtree it is currently generating or being trained on.

Reasoning models.

We train the reasoning model from scratch in a supervised fashion, by manually inserting the desired memory states periodically in the training data. For instance, suppose that we aim at a reasoning model p(⋅∣−)p(\cdot\mid-) as in Equation 4 capable of exact sampling. We generate a sequence

L0,M0,L1,M1,…,Ldh−w,Mdh−wL_{0},M_{0},L_{1},M_{1},\ldots,L_{d^{h-w}},M_{d^{h-w}}

where (Li+1,Mi+1)(L_{i+1},M_{i+1}) are sampled from p(⋅∣Li,Mi)p(\cdot\mid L_{i},M_{i}) autoregressively, tokenize the sequence, randomly sample a chunk of length kk, and feed it as a training sample. To inform the model wrapper that part of the output is the memory state and not the actual leaves, we prepend and append special memory tokens to mark the beginning and the end of the memory section.

4.1 Ising Broadcast Process

We collect the dhd^{h} spins autoregressively outputted by the models and compute their sum ∑Xr\sum X_{r}. We repeat this at least 1,000 times and visualize distributional properties of ∑Xr\sum X_{r}. To compare with the theory results in Section 3.1, we estimate the log-normalized variances as predicted in by Equation 1 in Theorem 3.1, as well as the excess kurtosis as in Equation 3 as predicted in Theorem 3.2.

We run the experiments with correlation ρ=0.9\rho=0.9 on ternary trees (d=3d=3) of height h=8h=8, so we are above the Kesten–Stigum threshold (d​ρ2=2.43>1d\rho^{2}=2.43>1). We train reasoning models with context sizes 26,27,⋯,2112^{6},2^{7},\cdots,2^{11} and non-reasoning models with context sizes 24,25,⋯,2112^{4},2^{5},\cdots,2^{11}. The results are summarized in Figure 1. The “Simulated” curve is computed using the true autoregressive broadcast process, with context depth ww defined in Definition 2.2. For the non-reasoning models, as context size decreases, the variance and the kurtosis deviate from the ground truth and converge to our asymptotic prediction as ww shrinks. In contrast, for reasoning models the variance and kurtosis are close to the ground truth even at context size 26=64≪dh=65612^{6}=64\ll d^{h}=6561.

4.2 Coloring Broadcast Process

In the qq-coloring model, we collect the dhd^{h} colors from the model output, and attempt to find a dd-ary tree with height hh with proper qq-coloring such that the colors of the leaves are those generated by the model. We repeat this at least 1000 times and count the number of successful reconstruction attempts to estimate the success rate.

We run the experiments with quaternary trees (d=4d=4) of height h=6h=6 on q=3q=3 colors, lying in the frozen regime. Context sizes are as in the Ising case. As shown in Figure 2, non-reasoning models with small context size almost never generate a sequence of valid colors, while the reasoning models almost always generate a valid sequence.

5 Limitations

A key advantage of our hierarchical model of language is to enable clean theory and empirical validation. It would be interesting to study both theoretically and empirically similar phenomena in natural languages. For our theoretical results, we leverage the geometry of regular trees to obtain precise quantitative predictions. Extending this theory to more general language or correlation structures is an interesting future direction.

Appendix A Overview of the Appendix

For our theoretical results, we introduce the relevant background from Markov chains and the theory of broadcast processes in Appendix B. In Appendix C, we carry out the asymptotic calculations for the ground truth Ising language using recursive arguments from the hierarchical structure. We build on this in Appendix D to make our theoretical predictions for autoregressive generation in the Ising (soft-constrained) version of our language. In Appendix E we prove that for the coloring (hard-constrained) version of our language, short-context models without reasoning will typically produce invalid trees, building on the freezing phenomenon in this model. In Appendix F, we complete the proof of the positive theoretical result for the reasoning model.

In Appendix G we give more details about the setup for our simulations with transformer models. In Appendix H, we state and prove some lemmas for asymptotic series calculations which are used in the proofs of our main results.

Appendix B Further Preliminaries

B.1 Markov Chains

In many of our arguments, we will use the information-theoretic characterization of Markov chains (see e.g. Cover and Thomas (2006)). Formally, a sequence of random variables A1,A2,…,AnA_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{n} forms a Markov chain, denoted

A1→A2→…→An,A_{1}\to A_{2}\to\ldots\to A_{n},

if for each kk, conditioned on AkA_{k}, the random variables (A1,…,Ak−1)(A_{1},\ldots,A_{k-1}) and (Ak+1,…,An)(A_{k+1},\ldots,A_{n}) are conditionally independent. In other words, the future and past of a Markov chain are conditionally independent given the present. An well-known equivalent definition is that the conditional distribution of AkA_{k} given A1,…,Ak−1A_{1},\ldots,A_{k-1} is the same as the conditional distribution of AkA_{k} given just Ak−1A_{k-1}.

It will be convenient to track several induced Markov chains in the autoregressive Ising process as in Definition 2.2 later on. We have the following highly convenient closed form for their cross-correlations for any Markov chain on marginally uniform spins:

Lemma B.1.

Let A1→…→AnA_{1}\to\ldots\to A_{n} denote any Markov chain with each Ai∈{±1}A_{i}\in\{\pm 1\} marginally uniform. Let αi=𝔼⁡[Ai​Ai+1]\alpha_{i}=\mathbb{E}[A_{i}A_{i+1}]. Then

𝔼⁡[A1​An]=∏i=1n−1αi\mathbb{E}[A_{1}A_{n}]=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\alpha_{i}
Proof.

This immediately follows by induction using the Markov property: the claim is trivially true for n=2n=2 and for general nn,

𝔼⁡[A1​An]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[A_{1}A_{n}] =𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[A1​An|An−1]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[A_{1}A_{n}|A_{n-1}]]
=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[A1|An−1]​𝔼​[An|An−1]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[A_{1}|A_{n-1}]\mathbb{E}[A_{n}|A_{n-1}]]
=αn−1​𝔼​[An−1​𝔼​[A1|An−1]]\displaystyle=\alpha_{n-1}\mathbb{E}[A_{n-1}\mathbb{E}[A_{1}|A_{n-1}]]
=αn−1​𝔼​[𝔼⁡[A1​An−1|An−1]]\displaystyle=\alpha_{n-1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[A_{1}A_{n-1}|A_{n-1}]]
=αn−1​𝔼​[A1​An−1],\displaystyle=\alpha_{n-1}\mathbb{E}[A_{1}A_{{n-1}}],

so we can conclude by induction. The second line follows by conditional independence in any Markov chain, while the rest is basic properties of binary random variables and conditional expectation. ∎

B.2 Broadcast Processes

In this section, we record simple calculations for dd-ary trees as well as relevant background on broadcasting processes that will be important in our arguments.

B.2.1 dd-ary Trees

For our computations, we will require the following distribution of least common ancestor heights in Td,hT_{d,h}.

Proposition B.2.

In Td,hT_{d,h}, for any leaf node ℓ\ell, the number of leaves in Td,hT_{d,h} whose least common ancestor with ℓ\ell is at distance kk is 11 for k=0k=0 and (dk−dk−1)(d^{k}-d^{k-1}) for 1≤k≤h1\leq k\leq h.

Proof.

This is immediate from the fact that all leaves at distance k>0k>0 from ℓ\ell are precisely the leaves belonging to the same subtree as ℓ\ell of size dkd^{k} but that do not belong to the same subtree of rr of size dk−1d^{k-1}. ∎

We will also need the following simple computation on the height of least common ancestors of a random adjacent pair of leaves (ℓ,ℓ+1)(\ell,\ell+1) where ℓ\ell is uniform on [d]h∖{(d,…,d)}[d]^{h}\setminus\{(d,\ldots,d)\}. Recall that under our encoding of the leaves, this excluded vertex is simply the rightmost vertex of Td,hT_{d,h}.

Proposition B.3.

Let 𝒟h\mathcal{D}_{h} denote the (random) height of the least common ancestor of a random pair of adjacent leaves (ℓ,ℓ+1)(\ell,\ell+1) sampled uniformly in Td,hT_{d,h}. Then as h→∞h\to\infty, the law of 𝒟h\mathcal{D}_{h} converges in distribution to 𝖦𝖾𝗈𝗆⁡(1/d)\mathsf{Geom}(1/d), a geometric random variable with success probability 1/d1/d.

In particular, for any fixed ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1),

αh:=𝔼s∼𝒟h​[ρ2​s]→α∗:=𝔼s∼𝖦𝖾𝗈𝗆⁡(1/d)​[ρ2​s]<1.\alpha_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}_{h}}[\rho^{2s}]\to\alpha^{*}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathsf{Geom}(1/d)}[\rho^{2s}]<1.
Proof.

Under our encoding of the tree, the least common ancestor of a pair (ℓ,ℓ+1)∈([d]h)2(\ell,\ell+1)\in([d]^{h})^{2} is precisely the last component of ℓ∈[d]h∖{(d,…,d)}\ell\in[d]^{h}\setminus\{(d,\ldots,d)\} that is not equal to dd since then there is no carryover. We can couple the sampling of ℓ\ell uniform on [d]h∖{(d,…,d)}[d]^{h}\setminus\{(d,\ldots,d)\} with a uniform sample on [d]h[d]^{h} up to error 1/dh1/d^{h} from sampling ℓ=(d,…,d)\ell=(d,\ldots,d). As h→∞h\to\infty, this probability of failure tends to 00, and moreover, the index of the last component that is not equal to dd converges to 𝖦𝖾𝗈𝗆⁡(1/d)\mathsf{Geom}(1/d) since each component then is equal to dd with probability 1/d1/d independently across coordinates. ∎

B.2.2 Ising Broadcast

Consider the Ising broadcast process on Td,hT_{d,h} with correlation parameter ρ\rho as in Definition 2.1. We will view d,ρd,\rho as fixed while h→∞h\to\infty. For our later computations to compute moments of the autoregressive Ising broadcast, we will need to define:

qh:=qh​(d,ρ)=𝔼⁡[𝔼​[X|Y]2]q_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=q_{h}(d,\rho)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y]^{2}]

where (X,Y)(X,Y) is the root and leaves, respectively, of a sample from the broadcast process on Td,hT_{d,h} with correlation ρ\rho. In other words, this is the (squared) expected reconstruction advantage on average over the sampling of the leaves. A fundamental fact from the theory of Ising broadcast processes is that when d​ρ2<1d\rho^{2}<1, then qh→0q_{h}\to 0 as h→∞h\to\infty while above the Kesten-Stigum bound, the reconstruction probability stays bounded away from 0:

Theorem B.4 (Kesten-Stigum Bound (Kesten and Stigum (1966a)), see e.g. Bleher et al. (1995)).

Consider the Ising broadcast process on Td,hT_{d,h} with correlation parameter ρ\rho and uniform prior on the root. Then if d​ρ2>1d\rho^{2}>1 is fixed, it holds that

limh→∞qh=q∗>0\lim_{h\to\infty}q_{h}=q^{*}>0

for an absolute constant q∗=q∗​(d,ρ)q^{*}=q^{*}(d,\rho).

Proof.

First, note that the limit exists because qhq_{h} is monotone non-increasing in hh. This is because the broadcast process can be written as a Markov chain

X→Y1→Y2→…→Yh,X\to Y^{1}\to Y^{2}\to\ldots\to Y^{h},

where YjY^{j} is the vector of spins at level jj of the dd-ary tree. In particular, the process for t≥1t\geq 1 defined by

𝔼⁡[X|Yt]\mathbb{E}[X|Y^{t}]

forms a backwards martingale. In particular, the L2L^{2}-norms are decreasing since

qt+1=𝔼⁡[𝔼​[X|Yt+1]2]=𝔼⁡[𝔼​[𝔼⁡[X|Yt]|Yt+1]2]≤𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[𝔼​[X|Yt]2|Yt+1]]=𝔼⁡[𝔼​[X|Yt]2]=qt,q_{t+1}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y^{t+1}]^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y^{t}]|Y^{t+1}]^{2}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y^{t}]^{2}|Y_{t+1}]]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X|Y^{t}]^{2}]=q_{t},

by Cauchy-Schwarz and the tower law. Therefore, qh→q∗q_{h}\to q^{*} for some q∗≥0q^{*}\geq 0 by nonnegativity.

To see that q∗q^{*} is in fact strictly positive when above the Kesten-Stigum bound, it is well-known (see e.g. Bleher et al. (1995)) that when d​ρ2>1d\rho^{2}>1, the following reconstruction problem is solvable (Mossel and Peres (2003)):

limh→∞dT​V​(Y1h,Y−1h)>0,\lim_{h\to\infty}d_{TV}(Y^{h}_{1},Y^{h}_{-1})>0, (5)

where Y1h,Y−1hY^{h}_{1},Y^{h}_{-1} denote the distributions of the leaves of the Ising broadcast process of depth hh conditioned on the root XX being +1+1 and −1-1, respectively. By definition of total variation distance,

dT​V​(Y1h,Y−1h)\displaystyle d_{TV}(Y^{h}_{1},Y^{h}_{-1}) =12​∑Yh∈{±1}dh|Pr⁡(Yh|X=1)−Pr⁡(Yh|X=−1)|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{Y^{h}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d^{h}}}|\Pr(Y^{h}|X=1)-\Pr(Y^{h}|X=-1)|
=∑Yh∈{±1}dhPr⁡(Yh)​|Pr⁡(X=1|Yh)−Pr⁡(X=−1|Yh)|\displaystyle=\sum_{Y^{h}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d^{h}}}\Pr(Y^{h})|\Pr(X=1|Y^{h})-\Pr(X=-1|Y^{h})|
=𝔼Yh​[|𝔼⁡[X|Yh]|]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y^{h}}\left[|\mathbb{E}[X|Y^{h}\right]|]
≤qh.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{q_{h}}.

The second equality is Bayes’ rule to rewrite the total variation distance in terms of the expected magnetization of the root given the leaves, and the final step is Cauchy-Schwarz. Since the total variation distance stays bounded away from zero above the KS bound by Equation 5, the same therefore holds true for qhq_{h} and hence the limiting value q∗q^{*}. ∎

B.2.3 Coloring Broadcast

A well-known fact for the coloring broadcast process is the onset of freezing: if the branching factor dd of Td,hT_{d,h} is sufficiently large compared to the number of colors qq, then with high probability over the sampling of the process, the posterior distribution of the root given the leaves is fixed to a unique color. We will require the following quantitative version by Sly (2009) that was implicit in earlier work of Mossel and Peres (2003) as well as Semerjian (2008):

Theorem B.5 (Freezing, Lemma 7 of Sly (2009)).

Consider the coloring broadcast process on Td,hT_{d,h} with qq colors. Then if the branching factor dd satisfies

d≥q⁡(log⁡(q)+log⁡log⁡(q)+oq​(1)),d\geq q(\log(q)+\log\log(q)+o_{q}(1)),

then if XL∈[q]dhX_{L}\in[q]^{d^{h}} denotes the colors of the leaves, then with probability at least 1−1/log⁡(q)1-1/\log(q) over XLX_{L}:

Law⁡(X∅|XL)=δi,\mathrm{Law}(X_{\emptyset}|X_{L})=\delta_{i},

where i∼[q]i\sim[q] is a marginally uniform color.

Appendix C Moments of the Ising Language

In this section, we compute important statistics of the Ising broadcast process so as to compare with the statistics of the autoregressive version that uses bounded context windows in generation. In particular, we will compute various moments of these processes that will be used for the proof of Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2.

C.1 Moments of the Broadcast Process

Throughout this section, we will consider the Ising broadcast process with correlation parameter ρ\rho satisfying d​ρ2=λ>1d\rho^{2}=\lambda>1; we will view dd and ρ\rho as fixed. We remark that a well-known equivalent description of the broadcast process is that with probability ρ\rho, an internal vertex copies its sign in Σ\Sigma to a child, while with probability 1−ρ1-\rho, it broadcasts a uniformly random sign.

To set up various recurrences, we will compute the following moments:

Md,ρ,h​(k):=𝔼⁡[(∑i∈[d]hXi)k|X∅=+1],M_{d,\rho,h}(k)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in[d]^{h}}X_{i}\right)^{k}\bigg|X_{\emptyset}=+1\right],

where XiX_{i} for i∈[d]hi\in[d]^{h} are the nodes at level hh of the broadcast process and X∅X_{\emptyset} is the value of the root. While our focus will eventually k=2,4k=2,4, this more general definition will enable us to recurse using the tree structure, and so here we will treat hh as a general variable in the recursion. Note that Md,ρ,h​(k)M_{d,\rho,h}(k) for kk even is the same as the unconditional expectation by symmetry. We will find that these moments are equal to (d​ρ)k​h(d\rho)^{kh} up to an explicit multiplicative constant depending only on d,ρd,\rho, but not hh.

The first two moments are well-known and elementary:

Proposition C.1.

Md,ρ,h​(2)=dh+dh⋅(1−1/d)⋅∑ℓ=1h(d​ρ2)ℓ.\displaystyle M_{d,\rho,h}(2)=d^{h}+d^{h}\cdot(1-1/d)\cdot\sum_{\ell=1}^{h}(d\rho^{2})^{\ell}.

The first moment is trivial from linearity of expectation. Each XrX_{r} for r∈[d]hr\in[d]^{h} has the same marginal distribution by symmetry, and has conditional expectation +1+1 when the path of length hh from the root has no re-randomizations, while is otherwise mean zero. This means

Md,ρ,h​(1)=dh⋅ρh=(d​ρ)h.M_{d,\rho,h}(1)=d^{h}\cdot\rho^{h}=(d\rho)^{h}.

Here, we use the fact that XℓX_{\ell} and Xℓ′X_{\ell^{\prime}} have nontrivial correlation if and only if the signal from their least common ancestor propagates to both of them, which occurs with probability ρ2​𝖫𝖢𝖠​(ℓ,ℓ′)\rho^{2\mathsf{LCA}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})} by independence in the broadcasting along edges. If this does not occur, then the root of the subtree is rerandomized and the expectation is zero by symmetry since we are computing an odd moment.

Appendix D Moments of the Autoregressive Ising Process

In this section, we complete the proof of Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2. To do this, we use the results of the previous section to compute moments for the autoregressive Ising process as defined in Definition 2.2. The main difference is that the cross-correlations will decay much faster even when above the Kesten-Stigum bound, so that the moments add up almost independently.

Recall that to generate the leaves of a new subtree YiY_{i} of size dwd^{w} in the autoregressive process given Yi−1Y_{i-1}, we sample the height hih_{i} from the law of heights of adjacent subtrees at depth h−wh-w in Td,hT_{d,h} and then sample YiY_{i} from the conditional law on (Yi−1,Yi)(Y_{i-1},Y_{i}) from the broadcast process when these subtrees have least common ancestor at height hih_{i}. This distribution over heights was considered in Proposition B.3.

Define α=αh−w=𝔼⁡[ρ2​h′]\alpha=\alpha_{h-w}=\mathbb{E}[\rho^{2h^{\prime}}], where h′h^{\prime} is sampled from the random height distribution 𝒟h−w\mathcal{D}_{h-w} of adjacent subtrees at depth h−wh-w. By Proposition B.3, we know that α→α∗\alpha\to\alpha^{*} as defined there as h−w→∞h-w\to\infty. Throughout the following results, we similarly define

Zi:=∑ℓ=1dw(Yi)ℓZ_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{d^{w}}(Y_{i})_{\ell}

for the sum of the leaves in the iith generated subtree of size dwd^{w}.

D.1 Equivalent Markov Chains

For our computations, we will use the following equivalent description of the AR process from the iith subtree leaves YiY_{i} to the i+ji+jth subtree leaves Yi+jY_{i+j}. Because YiY_{i} is marginally a sample from the normal broadcast process, we can equivalently sample this process via the following Markov chain:

Yi→Xi→Xi+1→Yi+1→Xi+1′→Xi+2→Yi+2→…→Yi+j−1→Xi+j−1′→Xi+j→Yi+j,Y_{i}\to X_{i}\to X_{i+1}\to Y_{i+1}\to X_{i+1}^{\prime}\to X_{i+2}\to Y_{i+2}\to\ldots\to Y_{i+j-1}\to X^{\prime}_{i+j-1}\to X_{i+j}\to Y_{i+j}, (6)

where XℓX_{\ell} is the root of the ℓ\ellth subtree; note that the actual AR process is only the restriction to the YℓY_{\ell} part. To sample XiX_{i} as well as each Xi+ℓ′X_{i+\ell}^{\prime} for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, we sample the posterior of the root of the corresponding subtree given the leaves in the previous step of the Markov chain (i.e. YiY_{i} and Yi+ℓY_{i+\ell}, respectively). The transition Xi→Xi+1X_{i}\to X_{i+1} as well as each Xi+ℓ′→Xi+ℓ+1X^{\prime}_{i+\ell}\to X_{i+\ell+1} for j≥1j\geq 1 is obtained by sampling the height hi+ℓh_{i+\ell} of the LCA of the subtrees and then rerandomizing the spin except with probability ρ2​hi+ℓ\rho^{2h_{i+\ell}}. Taken on average over hi+ℓ∼𝒟h−wh_{i+\ell}\sim\mathcal{D}_{h-w}, this means that the probability of not rerandomizing is precisely 𝔼⁡[Xi+ℓ′​Xi+ℓ+1]=α\mathbb{E}[X^{\prime}_{i+\ell}X_{i+\ell+1}]=\alpha, which we know converges to α∗\alpha^{*} as h−w→∞h-w\to\infty by Proposition B.3.22 2 Note that the difference in the first step of this Markov chain comes from the fact that conditioned on hih_{i}, the marginal on (Yi,Yi+1)(Y_{i},Y_{i+1}) is the same as an honest sample from the broadcast process from a root that connects to the root of each subtree at distance hih_{i} in each branch; in other words, we need not sample Xi′X_{i}^{\prime} since conditioned on YiY_{i}, it has the same law as XiX_{i} itself so we may rewrite in this way.

D.2 Preliminary Calculations

In the remaining computations, we will leverage the following highly convenient fact: for a pair of random variables (X1,X2)∈{±1}2(X_{1},X_{2})\in\{\pm 1\}^{2} that are marginally uniform, if 𝔼⁡[X1​X2]=γ≥0\mathbb{E}[X_{1}X_{2}]=\gamma\geq 0, then one can equivalently sample them by sampling X1X_{1} uniformly and then setting X2=X1X_{2}=X_{1} with probability γ\gamma and otherwise setting X2X_{2} to be a uniform bit. We will refer to this latter event, which occurs with 1−γ1-\gamma probability, as rerandomizing.

Next, we will calculate the correlations of the root values of the generated subtrees in the autoregressive process as expressed in the equivalent Markov chain given in Equation 6.

Lemma D.1.

Fix any i≥1i\geq 1 and let j≥1j\geq 1. Then for the Markov chain given in Equation 6,

𝔼⁡[Xi​Xi+j]=α​(α​qw)j−1.\mathbb{E}[X_{i}X_{i+j}]=\alpha(\alpha q_{w})^{j-1}.
Proof.

If j=1j=1, then by the Markov representation in Equation 6, we have:

Yi→Xi→Xi+1→Yi+1Y_{i}\to X_{i}\to X_{i+1}\to Y_{i+1}

is a Markov chain, and in particular, the probability that there is no rerandomization from Xi→Xi+1X_{i}\to X_{i+1} is α\alpha. Since these bits are marginally uniform, this means 𝔼⁡[Xi​Xi+1]=α\mathbb{E}[X_{i}X_{i+1}]=\alpha.

For j>1j>1, observe that we can consider the restriction in Equation 6 to the Markov chain on subtree root spins in {±1}\{\pm 1\} given by

Xi→Xi+1→Xi+2→…→Xi+j.X_{i}\to X_{i+1}\to X_{i+2}\to\ldots\to X_{i+j}.

Since these spins are binary and marginally uniform, Lemma B.1 implies that

𝔼⁡[Xi​Xi+j]=∏k=1jαk,\mathbb{E}[X_{i}X_{i+j}]=\prod_{k=1}^{j}\alpha_{k},

where αk=𝔼⁡[Xi+k−1​Xi+k]\alpha_{k}=\mathbb{E}[X_{i+k-1}X_{i+k}]. Therefore, it suffices for us to compute αk\alpha_{k} for k≥2k\geq 2 since we already know α1=α\alpha_{1}=\alpha.

To do this, observe that we again have the restriction to a Markov chain on {±1}\{\pm 1\} with uniform marginals:

Xi+k−1→Xi+k−1′→Xi+k,X_{i+k-1}\to X^{\prime}_{i+k-1}\to X_{i+k},

where by the above discussion,

𝔼⁡[Xi+k−1′​Xi+k]=𝔼⁡[ρ2​hi+k−1]=α\mathbb{E}[X^{\prime}_{i+k-1}X_{i+k}]=\mathbb{E}[\rho^{2h_{i+k-1}}]=\alpha

since this comes only from the sampling of the random height hi+kh_{i+k} and then rerandomizing except with probability ρ2​hi+k\rho^{2h_{i+k}} between the roots of these adjacent subtrees. By Lemma B.1, it therefore suffices to compute

𝔼⁡[Xi+k−1​Xi+k−1′]\mathbb{E}[X_{i+k-1}X_{i+k-1}^{\prime}]

from the AR process, which we can write as the induced Markov chain Xi+k−1→Yi+k−1→Xi+k−1′X_{i+k-1}\to Y_{i+k-1}\to X^{\prime}_{i+k-1}. To do this, observe that conditional on Yi+k−1Y_{i+k-1}, Xi+k−1X_{i+k-1} and Xi+k−1′X_{i+k-1}^{\prime} are independent posterior samples of the subtree root value XX given these leaves, and so

𝔼⁡[Xi+k−1​Xi+k−1′]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[X_{i+k-1}X_{i+k-1}^{\prime}] =𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Xi+k−1​Xi+k−1′|Yi+k−1]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X_{i+k-1}X_{i+k-1}^{\prime}|Y_{i+k-1}]]
=𝔼⁡[𝔼​[Xi+k−1|Yi+k−1]2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X_{i+k-1}|Y_{i+k-1}]^{2}]
=qw.\displaystyle=q_{w}.

Putting these two steps together, Lemma B.1 therefore implies that for k>1k>1,

αk\displaystyle\alpha_{k} =𝔼⁡[Xi+k−1​Xi+k]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[X_{i+k-1}X_{i+k}]
=α⋅qw,\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot q_{w},

which completes the proof. ∎

We now use this explicit expression for the correlations of root spins in the AR process to calculate the correlations of subtree sums by leveraging conditional independencies once we condition on these spins:

Lemma D.2.

In the autoregressive broadcast process, for any i,j≥1i,j\geq 1, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Yi​Yi+j]=Md,ρ,w​(1)2⋅α⋅(α⋅qw)j−1.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}Y_{i+j}]=M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{2}\cdot\alpha\cdot(\alpha\cdot q_{w})^{j-1}.
Proof.

We have that

Zi→Xi→Xi+j→Zi+jZ_{i}\to X_{i}\to X_{i+j}\to Z_{i+j}

is a Markov chain. Since 𝔼⁡[Xi​Xi+j]=α⋅(α⋅qw)j−1\mathbb{E}[X_{i}X_{i+j}]=\alpha\cdot(\alpha\cdot q_{w})^{j-1} by Lemma D.1, the probability that the transition Xi→Xi+jX_{i}\to X_{i+j} does not rerandomize is precisely α⋅(α⋅qw)j−1\alpha\cdot(\alpha\cdot q_{w})^{j-1}; moreover, note that this event is independent of the actual value of XiX_{i} by symmetry and therefore also ZiZ_{i} since the process is a Markov chain. If ℰ\mathcal{E} is the event that this rerandomization event occurs, then by the tower law

𝔼[ZiZi+j|ℰ]=𝔼[Zi𝔼[Zi+j|ℰ,Yi]|ℰ]=0\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{i+j}|\mathcal{E}]=\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}\mathbb{E}[Z_{i+j}|\mathcal{E},Y_{i}]|\mathcal{E}]=0

since the subtree root Xi+jX_{i+j} is then a uniform root bit conditioned on YiY_{i} and ℰ\mathcal{E}. On the other hand, when ℰ\mathcal{E} does not occur, we know that Xi=Xi+jX_{i}=X_{i+j}. Then

𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj|ℰc]=𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj|Xi=Xj]=Xi2​(Md,ρ,w​(1))2=(Md,ρ,w​(1))2,\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}|\mathcal{E}^{c}]=\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}|X_{i}=X_{j}]=X_{i}^{2}(M_{d,\rho,w}(1))^{2}=(M_{d,\rho,w}(1))^{2},

since in this case, the Markov property implies Yi,Yi+jY_{i},Y_{i+j} are conditionally independent samples from the broadcast process but with common root value XiX_{i}. The claim then follows by the law of total probability as

𝔼⁡[Zi​Zi+j]=Pr⁡(ℰ)⋅0+Pr⁡(ℰc)⋅(Md,ρ​(1))2=Md,ρ​(1)2⋅α⋅(α⋅qw)j−1.\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{i+j}]=\Pr(\mathcal{E})\cdot 0+\Pr(\mathcal{E}^{c})\cdot(M_{d,\rho}(1))^{2}=M_{d,\rho}(1)^{2}\cdot\alpha\cdot(\alpha\cdot q_{w})^{j-1}.

∎

We now compute the higher cross-moments that will be needed for calculating the fourth moment of the autoregressive process. The first bound is trivial:

Lemma D.3.

In the AR process, for any ii, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Zi2]=Md,w,ρ​(2)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}]=M_{d,w,\rho}(2)
𝔼⁡[Zi4]=Md,w,ρ​(4)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{4}]=M_{d,w,\rho}(4)
Proof.

This is trivial since YiY_{i} has the same distribution as the usual broadcast process of depth ww. ∎

Lemma D.4.

In the AR process, for any i<j<ki<j<k, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Zi2​Zj​Zk]=α⋅(α​qw)k−j−1​Md,ρ,w​(2)⋅Md,ρ,w​(1)2.\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}Z_{j}Z_{k}]=\alpha\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{k-j-1}M_{d,\rho,w}(2)\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{2}.

Similarly, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj​Zk2]=α⋅(α​qw)k−j−1​Md,ρ,w​(2)⋅Md,ρ,w​(1)2\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}Z_{k}^{2}]=\alpha\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{k-j-1}M_{d,\rho,w}(2)\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{2}
Proof.

We claim that conditioned on Zi2Z_{i}^{2}, (Yj,Yk)(Y_{j},Y_{k}) has the same law as in the AR process without any further conditioning. Indeed, note that conditioning on Yi2Y_{i}^{2} does not change the distribution of the root XiX_{i} by symmetry since the square makes the sum independent of the root value. This implies that the rest of the Markov chain has identical conditional distribution to the original Markov chain. Therefore,

𝔼⁡[Zi2​Zj​Zk]=𝔼⁡[Zi2]​𝔼​[Zj​Zk],\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}Z_{j}Z_{k}]=\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}]\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}Z_{k}],

and so, we may conclude by Lemma D.2 and the fact that YiY_{i} itself is simply a sample from the broadcast process with depth ww. An analogous argument holds for the second expectation since similarly, the distribution of Zk2Z_{k}^{2} is independent of (Yi,Yj)(Y_{i},Y_{j}) by symmetry after squaring. ∎

Lemma D.5.

In the AR process, for any i<j<k<ℓi<j<k<\ell, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj​Zk​Zℓ]=α2⋅(α​qw)(ℓ−k)+(j−i)−2⋅Md,ρ,w​(1)4.\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}Z_{k}Z_{\ell}]=\alpha^{2}\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{(\ell-k)+(j-i)-2}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{4}.
Proof.

Note that the restriction of the AR process

Yi→Yj→Xj′→Yk→Yℓ.Y_{i}\to Y_{j}\to X_{j}^{\prime}\to Y_{k}\to Y_{\ell}.

remains a Markov chain. To compute the expectation, we first condition on Xj′X_{j}^{\prime} to obtain

𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj|Xj′]​𝔼​[Zk​Zℓ|Xj′]],\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}|X_{j}^{\prime}]\mathbb{E}[Z_{k}Z_{\ell}|X_{j}^{\prime}]],

where we use the Markov property to decompose the conditionally independent parts as the subtree sums are functions of the corresponding leaves. However, observe that by symmetry, both expectations are independent of the value of Xj′X_{j}^{\prime} since as in the proof of Lemma D.2, the expectation is zero except on the event that there is no rerandomization. This is independent of the spin Xj′X_{j}^{\prime} by symmetry. In particular, we find that

𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj​Zk​Zℓ]=𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj]​𝔼​[Zk​Zℓ],\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}Z_{k}Z_{\ell}]=\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}]\mathbb{E}[Z_{k}Z_{\ell}],

and we conclude by Lemma D.2. ∎

Lemma D.6.

In the AR process, for any i<j<ki<j<k, it holds that

0≤𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj2​Zk]≤α2⋅(α​qw)(k−j)+(j−i)−2⋅Md,ρ,w​(1)2⋅Md,ρ,w​(2).0\leq\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}^{2}Z_{k}]\leq\alpha^{2}\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{(k-j)+(j-i)-2}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{2}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(2).
Proof.

We again have a Markov chain

Yi→Xi→Xj→Yj→Xj′→Xk→Yk.Y_{i}\to X_{i}\to X_{j}\to Y_{j}\to X^{\prime}_{j}\to X_{k}\to Y_{k}.

We claim that conditional on YjY_{j}, the probability there is no rerandomization between XiX_{i} and XkX_{k} is

α2⋅(α​qw)(k−j)+(j−i)−2⋅𝔼​[Xj|Yj]2.\alpha^{2}\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{(k-j)+(j-i)-2}\cdot\mathbb{E}[X_{j}|Y_{j}]^{2}.

Indeed, the conditional probability that there is no randomization between Xi→XjX_{i}\to X_{j} and from Xj′→XkX^{\prime}_{j}\to X_{k} is precisely α2⋅(α​qw)(k−j)+(j−i)−2\alpha^{2}\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{(k-j)+(j-i)-2} by Lemma D.1 since these events are independent of the actual value of YjY_{j} by the Markov property and spin symmetry. Moreover, the probability that there is no randomization between XjX_{j} and Xj′X^{\prime}_{j} given YjY_{j} is 𝔼​[Xj|Yj]2\mathbb{E}[X_{j}|Y_{j}]^{2} by the argument of Lemma D.1. If we let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the event that there is rerandomization between XiX_{i} and XkX_{k}, then similar computations to before imply

𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj2​Zk]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}^{2}Z_{k}] =𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj2​Zk|Yj]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}^{2}Z_{k}|Y_{j}]]
=𝔼⁡[Zj2​𝔼​[Zi​Zk|Yj]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}^{2}\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{k}|Y_{j}]]
=Md,ρ,w​(1)2⋅𝔼⁡[Zj2​Pr⁡(ℰc|Zj)]\displaystyle=M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}^{2}\Pr(\mathcal{E}^{c}|Z_{j})]
=α2⋅(α​qw)(k−j)+(j−i)−2⋅Md,ρ,w​(1)2⋅𝔼⁡[Zj2​𝔼​[Xj|Yj]2]\displaystyle=\alpha^{2}\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{(k-j)+(j-i)-2}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}[Z_{j}^{2}\mathbb{E}[X_{j}|Y_{j}]^{2}]
≤α2⋅(α​qw)(k−j)+(j−i)−2⋅Md,ρ,w​(1)2⋅Md,ρ,w​(2).\displaystyle\leq\alpha^{2}\cdot(\alpha q_{w})^{(k-j)+(j-i)-2}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1)^{2}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(2).

In the last step, we use the trivial fact that Xj∈{−1,1}X_{j}\in\{-1,1\} to pull out the factor. Note that this computation implies that the expectation is nonnegative since it admits a square representation. ∎

Lemma D.7.

In the AR process, for any i<ji<j, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Zi2​Zj2]=Md,w,ρ​(2)2.\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}Z_{j}^{2}]=M_{d,w,\rho}(2)^{2}.
Proof.

We again have a Markov chain

Yi→Xi→Xj→Yj.Y_{i}\to X_{i}\to X_{j}\to Y_{j}.

Conditioned on (Xi,Xj)(X_{i},X_{j}), YiY_{i} and YjY_{j} are conditionally independent, and moreover, the law of (Zi2,Zj2)(Z_{i}^{2},Z_{j}^{2}) is independent of (Xi,Xj)(X_{i},X_{j}) by symmetry since the subtree sums get squared and thus do not depend on the root values. The claim follows. ∎

Lemma D.8.

In the AR process, for any i<ji<j, it holds that

𝔼⁡[Zi3​Zj]=𝔼⁡[Zi​Zj3]=α⋅(α⋅qw)j−i−1⋅Md,ρ,w​(3)⋅Md,ρ,w​(1).\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{3}Z_{j}]=\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{j}^{3}]=\alpha\cdot(\alpha\cdot q_{w})^{j-i-1}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(3)\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1).
Proof.

We again have a Markov chain

Yi→Xi→Xj→Yj.Y_{i}\to X_{i}\to X_{j}\to Y_{j}.

By similar reasoning to Lemma D.2, let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the event that there is a rerandomization from Xi→XjX_{i}\to X_{j}. By Lemma D.1, the complementary event ℰc\mathcal{E}^{c} has probability α⋅(α⋅qw)j−i−1\alpha\cdot(\alpha\cdot q_{w})^{j-i-1} even conditioned on XiX_{i}. We again know that the conditional expectation of ZjZ_{j} given ℰ\mathcal{E} occurs and given YiY_{i} is zero, and moreover,

𝔼[Zi3Zj|ℰc,Xi]=Xi2⋅Md,ρ,w(3)⋅Md,ρ,w(1)=Md,ρ,w(3)⋅Md,ρ,w(1),\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{3}Z_{j}|\mathcal{E}^{c},X_{i}]=X_{i}^{2}\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(3)\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1)=M_{d,\rho,w}(3)\cdot M_{d,\rho,w}(1),

since on this event, the roots are identical and then one can apply conditional independence conditioned on having the same root. The claim again follows. ∎

D.3 Variance and Fourth Moments

At this point, we can use the cross-correlations computed in the previous section to compute the variance of the sum in the autoregressive process:

Proposition D.9.

Let XLX_{L} be sampled from the (d,h)(d,h)-Ising autoregressive broadcast process with fixed correlation ρ\rho satisfying d​ρ2>1d\rho^{2}>1 with w→∞w\to\infty and h−w→∞h-w\to\infty. Then

𝖵𝖺𝗋⁡(∑i=1dh(XL)i)=𝖵𝖺𝗋⁡(∑i=1dh−wZi)\displaystyle\mathsf{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d^{h}}(X_{L})_{i}\right)=\mathsf{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d^{h-w}}Z_{i}\right) =dh−w​Md,w​(2)+(1−o⁡(1))⋅2​α∗1−α∗​q∗⋅(d​ρ)2​w⋅dh−w\displaystyle=d^{h-w}M_{d,w}(2)+(1-o(1))\cdot\frac{2\alpha^{*}}{1-\alpha^{*}q^{*}}\cdot(d\rho)^{2w}\cdot d^{h-w}
=(1−o⁡(1))⋅Ad,ρ​(2)⋅(d​ρ)2​w⋅dh−w\displaystyle=(1-o(1))\cdot A_{d,\rho}(2)\cdot(d\rho)^{2w}\cdot d^{h-w}

where

Ad,ρ​(2):=(Cd,ρ​(2)+2​α∗1−α∗​q∗)A_{d,\rho}(2)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left(C_{d,\rho}(2)+\frac{2\alpha^{*}}{1-\alpha^{*}q^{*}}\right)
Proof.

We can directly compute:

Appendix E Inconsistent Colorings Above Freezing

We now turn to establishing that an autoregressive broadcast process for the coloring process will fail to produce a consistent coloring of the full dd-ary tree. By this, we mean that with high probability over the sampling of the autoregressive process, there is no proper coloring of the entire tree Td,hT_{d,h} that can be extended from the color of the sampled leaves. In fact, we will show that this holds even just to go up a single level of the tree.

To prove this, we require the following simple observation on the posterior distribution of a child of the root given any prior distribution on any other child:

Lemma E.1.

Consider the coloring broadcast process with qq colors on Td,hT_{d,h}. Let X∅X_{\emptyset} denote the color of the root of the tree and let X1,…,XdX_{1},\ldots,X_{d} denote the colors of the children. Then given any distribution ν\nu on the first child X1X_{1}, the posterior distribution on X2X_{2} is lower bounded by (q−2)/(q−1)2(q-2)/(q-1)^{2} for all colors.

Proof.

It suffices to show that the claim is true conditioned on any value of X1X_{1}. Given the color of X1∈[q]X_{1}\in[q], the posterior distribution on X∅X_{\emptyset} is simply uniform on [q]∖{X1}[q]\setminus\{X_{1}\}. Conditioned on any of these valid colors, the posterior distribution on X2X_{2} simply becomes uniform on [q]∖{X∅}[q]\setminus\{X_{\emptyset}\}. It is easy then to see that for any i∈[q]i\in[q], and initial choice of X1X_{1}, there are q−2q-2 choices of X∅X_{\emptyset} such the posterior probability Xi=iX_{i}=i is 1/(q−1)1/(q-1). Since each of these q−2q-2 choices for X∅X_{\emptyset} has probability at least 1/(q−1)1/(q-1) given X1X_{1}, the claim follows. ∎

We can now put this simple observation with the onset of freezing:

Theorem E.2 (Theorem 3.3, restated).

Consider the autoregressive coloring broadcast process with qq colors on Td,hT_{d,h} with any context depth w<hw<h such that d>q⁡(log⁡(q)+log⁡log⁡(q)+1+oq​(1))d>q(\log(q)+\log\log(q)+1+o_{q}(1)). Then with probability 1−oq​(1)1-o_{q}(1), the sampling of the leaves in the autoregressive coloring process is inconsistent with any proper coloring of Td,hT_{d,h}.

Proof.

Consider an internal vertex vv at depth h−w−1≥0h-w-1\geq 0. We will show that in the autoregressive coloring process for this range of parameters, it holds with 1−oq​(1)1-o_{q}(1) probability over the sampling of the dd subtrees of size dwd^{w} that there is no valid color for vertex vv.

Label the children of vv by 1,…,d1,\ldots,d at level h−wh-w. In the autoregressive sampling, we sample the subtree of i+1i+1 of size dwd^{w} given the colors of the subtree of ii. It is clear that marginally, the subtree of vertex 11 is a sample from the true coloring broadcast process of the dd-ary tree at depth ww, which can be obtained by sampling the color X1X_{1} uniformly and then running the broadcast process for this root value. We will consider the following equivalent description of the sampling process: to sample the (i+1)(i+1)th subtree given the value of the leaves of the iith subtree, we obtain the posterior distribution on XiX_{i}, which implies the posterior on Xi+1X_{i+1}, which is then broadcast to the leaves in the coloring process.

By Theorem B.5, it follows that in this sampling process that X1X_{1} is frozen to a uniformly random color i1∈[q]i_{1}\in[q] given the colors of its leaves with probability at least 1−1/log⁡(q)1-1/\log(q). More generally, using Theorem B.5 again and symmetry, the posterior of each XiX_{i} given the leaves of the iith subtree is again frozen to the actual value XiX_{i} given the colors of the leaves with probability at least 1−1/log⁡(q)1-1/\log(q), and by Lemma E.1, it further holds that each color XiX_{i} has probability at least (q−2)/(q−1)2(q-2)/(q-1)^{2} of being any i∈[q]i\in[q] for any conditioning of the previous subtree (which has an induced posterior ν\nu on Xi−1X_{i-1}).

We now claim that with 1−oq​(1)1-o_{q}(1) probability, this implies that there is no valid color for vertex vv that can be consistent with the colors of the dd sampled subtrees of this process. Indeed, this event is implied by the event that for each color i∈[q]i\in[q], there exists some XjX_{j} in this process that is frozen to color i∈[q]i\in[q] by the corresponding leaves of the subtree. By a standard coupon collector argument,

Pr\displaystyle\Pr (∃i∈[q]:i valid for v given leaves)\displaystyle\left(\exists i\in[q]\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\text{$i$ valid for $v$ given leaves}\right)
≤q​(1−(1−1/log⁡(q))​q−2(q−1)2)d\displaystyle\leq q\left(1-(1-1/\log(q))\frac{q-2}{(q-1)^{2}}\right)^{d}
≤qexp(−(1−O(1/q2))⋅d⁡(1−1/log⁡(q))q)\displaystyle\leq q\exp\left(-(1-O(1/q^{2}))\cdot\frac{d(1-1/\log(q))}{q}\right)
≤qexp(−(1−O(1/q2))⋅(log(q)+loglog(q)+1+oq(1))(1−1/log(q)))\displaystyle\leq q\exp\left(-(1-O(1/q^{2}))\cdot(\log(q)+\log\log(q)+1+o_{q}(1))(1-1/\log(q))\right)
≤q​exp⁡(−(1−O⁡(1/q2))​(log⁡(q)+log⁡log⁡(q)−oq​(1)))\displaystyle\leq q\exp(-(1-O(1/q^{2}))(\log(q)+\log\log(q)-o_{q}(1)))
=1+oq​(1)log⁡(q),\displaystyle=\frac{1+o_{q}(1)}{\log(q)},

as claimed. ∎

Remark E.1.

It appears unlikely that one can go below the freezing threshold and still obtain the same inconsistent colorings. The reason is simply because this bound is tight for freezing, and as soon as one is below it, the probability of freezing decays doubly exponentially in the height of the tree. This can be most easily seen when d=q−1d=q-1, in which case the probability a parent at depth h−1h-1 is frozen is on the order of e−qe^{-q}. Following the recursion, this causes the probability of a node at depth h−wh-w being inconsistent with the leaves to be exp⁡(−Θ⁡(qw))\exp(-\Theta(q^{w})), so it is actually doubly exponentially small in the depth. This can only be offset by the number of vertices for very small context depths ww to obtain an internal node that has no valid colors.

Appendix F Exponential Advantage of Reasoning

In this section, we give a proof of Theorem 3.4. We design an even simpler model where p(⋅∣−)p(\cdot\mid-) conditions only on the current memory state. Set ℳ=(Σh−w∪{∅})×[d]h−w\mathcal{M}=(\Sigma^{h-w}\cup\{\emptyset\})\times[d]^{h-w}. The Σh−w∪{∅}\Sigma^{h-w}\cup\{\emptyset\} component encodes the values along the path from the root of the entire tree to the root of the current subtree, and the [d]h−w[d]^{h-w} component encodes the index of the next subtree. We start with an initial memory state (∅,(1,⋯,1))(\emptyset,(1,\cdots,1)). Let M=(P,r)M=(P,r) be the current memory state, and we describe a procedure that samples the next leaves Y′Y^{\prime} and the next memory state M′=(P′,r′)M^{\prime}=(P^{\prime},r^{\prime}). The idea is to mimic the depth-first search of the tree defining the (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-language.

  1. 1.

    We first sample, if not already observed, the values along the path defined by rr in the current (d,h,κ)(d,h,\kappa)-broadcast process.

    • •

      If r=(1,⋯,1)r=(1,\cdots,1), then we recursively sample through the broadcast channel κ\kappa

      X∅,X(1),X(1,1),⋯,Xr.X_{\emptyset},X_{(1)},X_{(1,1)},\cdots,X_{r}\,.

      That is, X∅X_{\emptyset} is sampled from the stationary distribution of κ\kappa, and Xr[1:ℓ+1]X_{r[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\ell+1]} is sampled from κ(Xr[1:ℓ],⋅)\kappa(X_{r[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\ell]},\cdot) for each ℓ=0,1,⋯,h−w−1\ell=0,1,\cdots,h-w-1.

    • •

      Otherwise, let jj be the largest integer such that rj>1r_{j}>1. By the induction hypothesis which will be ensured later, the jjth component of PP equals the already observed Xr[1:j−1]X_{r[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}j-1]} (X∅X_{\emptyset} if j=1j=1). Starting from this, we recursively sample through the broadcast channel κ\kappa

      Xr[1:j],Xr[1:j+1],⋯,Xr.X_{r[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}j]},X_{r[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}j+1]},\cdots,X_{r}\,.
  2. 2.

    Now we have access to the values X∅,⋯,XrX_{\emptyset},\cdots,X_{r}. We sample a (d,w,κ,δXr)(d,w,\kappa,\delta_{X_{r}})-language and set Y′Y^{\prime} to be the sampled leaves. This is the broadcast process on Td,wT_{d,w} where the root has a fixed value XrX_{r}. Then we set

    P′=(X∅,⋯,Xr[1:h−w−1]).P^{\prime}=(X_{\emptyset},\cdots,X_{r[1\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}h-w-1]})\,.
  3. 3.

    Let kk be the largest integer such that rk<dr_{k}<d. We set

    r′=(r1,⋯,rk+1,1,⋯,1).r^{\prime}=(r_{1},\cdots,r_{k}+1,1,\cdots,1)\,.

As noted before, this can be understood as the depth-first sampling of a broadcast process and thus samples the correct language by construction.

Appendix G Experiment Details

G.1 Tokenization

We elaborate on a tokenization procedure of our synthetic language based on the broadcast model on dd-ary trees, as described in Definition 2.1. The first step is to tokenize the states in Σ\Sigma. Since the two broadcast processes we consider have discrete state spaces, we can simply use them as tokens. In addition, we insert “punctuation” tokens to encode the information of the least common ancestor of the two adjacent nodes. In other words, we use the token set 𝒯=Σ⊔𝒫\mathcal{T}=\Sigma\sqcup\mathcal{P} where 𝒫={p1,p2,⋯,ph−1}\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},p_{2},\cdots,p_{h-1}\} is the set of punctuation tokens. Before we mathematically define the tokenization procedure, we refer the reader to Figure 3 for a quick illustration on how we tokenize an Ising broadcast model.

The tokenization of Td,hT_{d,h} with leaves XrX_{r} for r∈[d]hr\in[d]^{h} is a sequence
