m=r0+(d+1)​∑i=1h−1(ri−1)​di−1m=r_{0}+(d+1)\sum_{i=1}^{h-1}(r_{i}-1)d^{i-1}

where ri∈[d]r_{i}\in[d] for 1≤i≤h−11\leq i\leq h-1 and 0≤r0≤d0\leq r_{0}\leq d. Note that there is a unique such expansion. Now τm\tau_{m} is given by:

τm={X(rh−1,⋯,r0)if r0≥1,pζ⁡(m)if r0=0\tau_{m}=\begin{cases}X_{(r_{h-1},\cdots,r_{0})}&\text{if $r_{0}\geq 1$,}\\ p_{\zeta(m)}&\text{if $r_{0}=0$}\end{cases}

where

ζ(m)=max{i∈ℤ+:rj=1 for all 1≤j<i}.\zeta(m)=\max\{i\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\text{$r_{j}=1$ for all $1\leq j<i$}\}\,.

G.2 Training Without Reasoning

We describe a procedure of preparing a training set to train a simple autoregressive model. Namely, given the context length kk, we explain how the pair of an input sequence 𝐱\mathbf{x} and an output sequence 𝐲\mathbf{y} is sampled. The model is trained using the usual cross entropy loss.

For efficient training, we add an additional “context refresh” token ∅\emptyset to the token set 𝒯~=𝒯∪{∅}\tilde{\mathcal{T}}=\mathcal{T}\cup\{\emptyset\}. This can also be understood as the “beginning of sequence” token. Now we sample 𝐱,𝐲∈𝒯~k\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\tilde{\mathcal{T}}^{k} with the following algorithm.

  1. 1.

    Sample an infinite sequence of independent broadcast processes: Td,h(1)T_{d,h}^{(1)} with leaves Xr(1)X_{r}^{(1)}, Td,h(2)T_{d,h}^{(2)} with leaves Xr(2)X_{r}^{(2)}, and so on.

  2. 2.

    Tokenize the processes which gives the sequences

    (τ1(1),⋯,τL(1)),(τ1(2),⋯,τL(2)),⋯.(\tau_{1}^{(1)},\cdots,\tau_{L}^{(1)}),(\tau_{1}^{(2)},\cdots,\tau_{L}^{(2)}),\cdots\,.
  3. 3.

    Join them with the context refresh token, giving an infinite sequence

    (τ~1,τ~2,⋯)=(τ1(1),⋯,τL(1),∅,τ1(2),⋯,τL(2),∅,τ1(3),⋯).(\tilde{\tau}_{1},\tilde{\tau}_{2},\cdots)=(\tau_{1}^{(1)},\cdots,\tau_{L}^{(1)},\emptyset,\tau_{1}^{(2)},\cdots,\tau_{L}^{(2)},\emptyset,\tau_{1}^{(3)},\cdots)\,.
  4. 4.

    Sample a random index ι∼Uniform⁡({1,⋯,L+1})\iota\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(\{1,\cdots,L+1\}) and obtain a consecutive subsequence

    τ~ι,τ~ι+1,⋯,τ~ι+k.\tilde{\tau}_{\iota},\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+1},\cdots,\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+k}\,.

    In particular, τ~ι=τι(1)\tilde{\tau}_{\iota}=\tau_{\iota}^{(1)} if ι≤L\iota\leq L and τ~ι=∅\tilde{\tau}_{\iota}=\emptyset otherwise.

  5. 5.

    Now set

    𝐱=(τ~ι,⋯,τ~ι+k−1),𝐲=(τ~ι+1,⋯,τ~ι+k).\mathbf{x}=(\tilde{\tau}_{\iota},\cdots,\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+k-1})\,,\qquad\mathbf{y}=(\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+1},\cdots,\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+k})\,.

For each backpropagation, a fresh pair of (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) is sampled from this procedure. This resembles the way the pre-training of large language models is usually done on large corpuses. In practice, the sequence (τ~1,⋯,)(\tilde{\tau}_{1},\cdots,) and the index ι\iota are not randomly sampled for each training step, but often ι\iota is just taken sequentially from a fixed sequence. In our experiments, however, the differences between the two approaches were insignificant.

The inference (sampling) step of the trained model is straightforward: we “prompt” the model with the context refresh token ∅\emptyset, sample the next token conditioned on the previous kk tokens, repeating LL times.

G.3 Training With Reasoning

As briefly noted in Section 4, the reasoning models are trained by inserting the “memory tokens” inbetween value tokens in the training set. Before we elaborate on this, it is helpful to describe the inference step, i.e., design a model “wrapper” that hides the memory tokens and outputs the value tokens in 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

We first choose positive integers ℓv\ell_{v} and ℓm\ell_{m} such that 2​ℓm+ℓv−12\ell_{m}+\ell_{v}-1 is at most the context size kk. We want the model to retain a memory of size ℓm\ell_{m} and output a sequence of ℓv\ell_{v} value tokens (including punctuation tokens) each step. To be specific, we want the model to perform the following sampling step: given its current memory state represented by ℓm\ell_{m} memory tokens, output ℓv\ell_{v} value tokens and ℓm\ell_{m} memory tokens representing the next memory state. This is why we require 2​ℓm+ℓv≤k+12\ell_{m}+\ell_{v}\leq k+1. We repeat this until the model has outputted LL tokens.

Markov chain of memory states.

The proof of Theorem 3.4 in Appendix F describes a way to design the memory state using the path from the root to the current position. The conditional distribution function constructed in the proof can be understood as the transition kernel of a Markov chain of memory states, where each transition from one state to another outputs a subtree of height ww. Our first step is to build a similar Markov chain so that it outputs a token one at a time. This requires a bit of extension since the model must be able to output a punctuation token. We set the memory states as the alternating sequences of values and indices of the form

σ1,r1,σ2,r2,⋯,σh−h0,rh−h0\sigma_{1},r_{1},\sigma_{2},r_{2},\cdots,\sigma_{h-h_{0}},r_{h-h_{0}} (8)

where σi∈Σ\sigma_{i}\in\Sigma, ri∈[d]r_{i}\in[d], and 0≤h0≤h0\leq h_{0}\leq h. This in particular means that the model has sampled

(X∅,Xr1,X(r1,r2),⋯,X(r1,⋯,rh−h0−1))=(σ1,⋯,σh−h0).(X_{\emptyset},X_{r_{1}},X_{(r_{1},r_{2})},\cdots,X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}-1})})=(\sigma_{1},\cdots,\sigma_{h-h_{0}})\,.

The state transition is defined as follows, depending on the value of h0h_{0}.

  • •

    The case h0=0h_{0}=0 is further divided into the following two.

    • –

      If rh<dr_{h}<d, then the model samples and outputs X(r1,⋯,rh+1)X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h}+1)} from X(r1,⋯,rh−1)=σhX_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-1})}=\sigma_{h} through the broadcast channel κ\kappa. The next state is a sequence

      σ1,r1,σ2,r2,⋯,σh,rh+1\sigma_{1},r_{1},\sigma_{2},r_{2},\cdots,\sigma_{h},r_{h}+1

      of the same length 2​h2h.

    • –

      If rh=dr_{h}=d, then the model computes the largest index j<hj<h such that rj<dr_{j}<d. If no such jj exists (i.e., ri=dr_{i}=d for all ii), then the model outputs a context refresh token ∅\emptyset and jumps to the state ∅\emptyset. Otherwise, the model outputs a punctuation token ph−jp_{h-j} and jumps to the state

      σ1,r1,⋯,σj,rj\sigma_{1},r_{1},\cdots,\sigma_{j},r_{j}

      which is a sequence of length 2​j2j.

  • •

    If 0<h0<h0<h_{0}<h, our construction guarantees rh−h0<dr_{h-h_{0}}<d. The model recursively samples

    X(r1,⋯,rh−h0+1),X(r1,⋯,rh−h0+1,1),⋯,X(r1,⋯,rh−h0+1,1,⋯,1)X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}}+1)},X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}}+1,1)},\cdots,X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}}+1,1,\cdots,1)}

    from X(r1,⋯,rh−h0−1)=σh−h0X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}-1})}=\sigma_{h-h_{0}} through κ\kappa, where the subscript of the last element has h0h_{0} ones. The model outputs X(r1,⋯,rh−h0+1,1,⋯,1)X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}}+1,1,\cdots,1)} and jumps to the state

    σ1,r1,⋯,σh−h0,rh−h0+1,X(r1,⋯,rh−h0+1),1,⋯,X(r1,⋯,rh−h0+1,1,⋯,1),1\sigma_{1},r_{1},\cdots,\sigma_{h-h_{0}},r_{h-h_{0}}+1,X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}}+1)},1,\cdots,X_{(r_{1},\cdots,r_{h-h_{0}}+1,1,\cdots,1)},1

    where the subscript of the penultimate element has h0−1h_{0}-1 ones.

  • •

    The case h0=hh_{0}=h corresponds to the initial and final state ∅\emptyset. The model samples

    X∅,X1,X(1,1),⋯,X(1,⋯,1)X_{\emptyset},X_{1},X_{(1,1)},\cdots,X_{(1,\cdots,1)}

    from a fresh tree, outputs the last value whose subscript has hh ones, and jump to the state

    X∅,1,⋯,X(1,⋯,1),1X_{\emptyset},1,\cdots,X_{(1,\cdots,1)},1

    where the subscript of the penultimate element has h−1h-1 ones.

Similar to the the argument in Appendix F, dh−1​(d+1)−1d^{h-1}(d+1)-1 state transitions starting from the initial memory state ∅\emptyset outputs the correct language distribution, including the punctuation marks.

Tokenization of the memory states.

Tokenizing the memory states Equation 8 is straightforward. We use the token set

𝒯m=Σ⊔[d]⊔{∅}⊔{s,e}\mathcal{T}_{m}=\Sigma\sqcup[d]\sqcup\{\emptyset\}\sqcup\{s,e\}

where ∅\emptyset is the optional “padding” token, which allows us to tokenize the memory states in a fixed length 2​h2h as

σ1,r1,⋯,σh−h0,rh−h0,∅,∅,⋯,∅,∅\sigma_{1},r_{1},\cdots,\sigma_{h-h_{0}},r_{h-h_{0}},\emptyset,\emptyset,\cdots,\emptyset,\emptyset

using 2​(h−h0)2(h-h_{0}) padding tokens. To prevent the model from confusing the memory state tokens with the output tokens, one might also choose to use different set of tokens for Σ\Sigma and ∅\emptyset. As discussed in Section 4, we also enclose the memory tokens with the additional “memory start token” ss and “memory end token” ee.

Recall that we want the model to generate ℓm\ell_{m} memory tokens every ℓv\ell_{v} output value tokens. Following the above tokenization of the memory states, we need ℓm=2+2​h\ell_{m}=2+2h tokens. As a consequence, we require that 1≤ℓv≤k−2​h−11\leq\ell_{v}\leq k-2h-1.

Constructing training sequences.

If the values of all of the nodes (including the internal nodes) of a tree Td,hT_{d,h} are given, then the Markov chain described in the previous paragraph becomes deterministic. In other words, it gives a unique sequence of memory states

∅=M0,M1,⋯,ML,ML+1=∅.\emptyset=M_{0},M_{1},\cdots,M_{L},M_{L+1}=\emptyset\,.

Now each training sequence is generated from the following procedure.

  1. 1.

    Sample an infinite sequence of independent broadcast processes Td,h(1),Td,h(2)T_{d,h}^{(1)},T_{d,h}^{(2)} and the corresponding sequences of memory states: for each Td,h(i)T_{d,h}^{(i)} we write

    ∅=M0(i),M1(i),⋯,ML+1(i)=∅\emptyset=M_{0}^{(i)},M_{1}^{(i)},\cdots,M_{L+1}^{(i)}=\emptyset

    for its sequence of memory states.

  2. 2.

    Following the same process in Section G.2 we obtain the sequence

    (τ~1,τ~2,⋯)=(τ1(1),⋯,τL(1),∅,τ1(2),⋯,τL(2),∅,τ1(3),⋯).(\tilde{\tau}_{1},\tilde{\tau}_{2},\cdots)=(\tau_{1}^{(1)},\cdots,\tau_{L}^{(1)},\emptyset,\tau_{1}^{(2)},\cdots,\tau_{L}^{(2)},\emptyset,\tau_{1}^{(3)},\cdots)\,.
  3. 3.

    Sample a random index ι∼Uniform⁡({1,⋯,L+1})\iota\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(\{1,\cdots,L+1\}) and consider the infinite sequence

    τ~ι,τ~ι+1,⋯.\tilde{\tau}_{\iota},\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+1},\cdots\,.
  4. 4.

    We insert ℓm=2+2​h\ell_{m}=2+2h tokens right before each of the tokens τ~ι,τ~ι+ℓv,τ~ι+2​ℓv,⋯\tilde{\tau}_{\iota},\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+\ell_{v}},\tilde{\tau}_{\iota+2\ell_{v}},\cdots. The memory tokens to insert before τ~s\tilde{\tau}_{s} are determined by the following. If s−1=(L+1)​i+js-1=(L+1)i+j for integers ii and 0≤j≤L0\leq j\leq L, we insert the tokenization of Mj(i+1)M_{j}^{(i+1)}.

  5. 5.

    Take the first k+1k+1 tokens from the new token sequence. Set 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐲\mathbf{y} to be the first kk and the last kk tokens from the chosen subsequence.

Note that 𝐱\mathbf{x} is an alternating sequence of ℓm\ell_{m} memory tokens and ℓv\ell_{v} output value tokens. Thus, the model learns to predict the next tokens given the first ℓm\ell_{m} memory tokens, and to maintain its memory state every ℓv\ell_{v} outputs.

G.4 Computing Resources and Reproducibility

Model hyperparameters.

Our base model nanochat, in its default configuration, automatically chooses its own model hyperparameters given the desired number of transformer layers and the context size. We use 1010 transformer layers for all of our experiments which is slightly larger than our maximum tree height 88. The weights of a model occupy less than 200 megabytes of disk storage.

Training iterations.

We configure to train 215=327682^{15}=32768 tokens in one mini-batch and 219=5242882^{19}=524288 tokens in one iteration. For instance, if the context size is 210=10242^{10}=1024, then 25=322^{5}=32 training sequences (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) are processed in one optimizer step and one training iteration always consists of 24=162^{4}=16 optimizer steps. We run 3,000 to 10,000 training iterations depending on the model we train.

Optimizer.

The optimizer we use is a combination of a modified Adam by Jordan et al. (2024a) and Muon by Jordan et al. (2024b). This is taken from the optimizer of the original nanochat by Karpathy (2025) without modification.

Computation.

We note that nanochat is powerful but lightweight enough to reach a GPT-2 grade capability for natural language in around 2 hours training on 8xH100 GPU node. Due to the simplicity of our synthetic language, all of the pre-training runs in our experiments take a few hours even with 2 A100 GPUs, which makes them easily reproducible. Approximately, 1,000 training iterations take about 1 hour of 2 A100 GPUs.

Context size for “Simulated” data points.

We note that for the “Simulated” data points in Figures 1 and 2, the context size is defined to be dw−1​(d+1)d^{w-1}(d+1), instead of dwd^{w}, because we properly take the punctuation marks into account.

Estimating variance and kurtosis.

Given the i.i.d. samples, these are computed using the standard sample variance and sample excess kurtosis formulae commonly available in scientific computing packages (see, e.g., Zwillinger and Kokoska (1999)).

Appendix H Auxiliary Results

Lemma H.1.

Let αn∈[0,1)\alpha_{n}\in[0,1) be a sequence that converges to some α∗<1\alpha^{*}<1. Then

∑1≤i<j<k≤nαnk−i=(1−o⁡(1))​(α∗1−α∗)2⋅n.\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}\alpha_{n}^{k-i}=(1-o(1))\left(\frac{\alpha^{*}}{1-\alpha^{*}}\right)^{2}\cdot n.
Proof.

Let s:=k−is\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=k-i and note that ss ranges from 22 to n−2n-2 under our index convention. For convenience, we will write α\alpha instead of αn\alpha_{n} below. Then by an elementary counting argument,

∑1≤i<j<k≤nαk−i=∑s=2n−2(n−s)​(s−1)​αs,\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}\alpha^{k-i}=\sum_{s=2}^{n-2}(n-s)(s-1)\alpha^{s},

since there are (n−s)(n-s) valid i<ki<k pairs with this difference, and for each such pair, there are exactly s−1s-1 valid indices jj for any such pair. We deduce that

∑1≤i<j<k≤nαk−i=n​∑s=2n−2αs​(s−1)−∑s=2n−2s⁡(s−1)​αs.\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}\alpha^{k-i}=n\sum_{s=2}^{n-2}\alpha^{s}(s-1)-\sum_{s=2}^{n-2}s(s-1)\alpha^{s}.

By the dominated convergence theorem (to be precise, αn<α′<1\alpha_{n}<\alpha^{\prime}<1 for all sufficiently large nn by the convergence assumption and the geometric series is bounded), the first sum converges with

limn→∞∑s=2n−2αs​(s−1)=∑s=2∞(s−1)​(α∗)s=(α∗1−α∗)2,\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{s=2}^{n-2}\alpha^{s}(s-1)=\sum_{s=2}^{\infty}(s-1)(\alpha^{*})^{s}=\left(\frac{\alpha^{*}}{1-\alpha^{*}}\right)^{2},

and similarly the second sum converges to a constant by standard bounds on geometric moments. ∎

Lemma H.2.

Let αn∈[0,1)\alpha_{n}\in[0,1) be a sequence that converges to some α∗<1\alpha^{*}<1. Then

∑1≤i<j<k≤nαnk−j=(1−o⁡(1))⋅α∗​n22​(1−α∗)\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}\alpha_{n}^{k-j}=(1-o(1))\cdot\frac{\alpha^{*}n^{2}}{2(1-\alpha^{*})}

.

Proof.

We again will write α\alpha in place of αn\alpha_{n}. By a similar combinatorial argument, we may write

∑1≤i<j<k≤nαk−j=∑s=1n−1(∑i=1n−s−1i)​αs=12​∑s=1n−1(n−s)​(n−s−1)​αs,\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}\alpha^{k-j}=\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-s-1}i\right)\alpha^{s}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}(n-s)(n-s-1)\alpha^{s},

since there are (n−s)(n-s) valid j<kj<k pairs with difference ss, and one may take all possible indices ii that are at most jj for each such pair leading to the inner sum. We can further simplify as

1n2​12​∑s=1n−1(n−s)​(n−s−1)​αs=12​∑s=1n−1(1−s/n)​(1−s/n−1/n)​αs.\displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}(n-s)(n-s-1)\alpha^{s}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}(1-s/n)(1-s/n-1/n)\alpha^{s}.

We may now take limits as n→∞n\to\infty. We can again apply dominated convergence using the convergence of αn→α∗\alpha_{n}\to\alpha^{*}, and so the limit of this sum is precisely

12​∑s=1∞(α∗)s=α∗2​(1−α∗),\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}(\alpha^{*})^{s}=\frac{\alpha^{*}}{2(1-\alpha^{*})},

which gives the desired conclusion. ∎

Lemma H.3.

Let αn∈[0,1)\alpha_{n}\in[0,1) be a sequence that converges to some α∗<1\alpha^{*}<1. Then

∑1≤i<j<k<ℓ≤nαn(ℓ−k)+(j−i)=(1−o⁡(1))⋅12⋅(α∗1−α∗)2⋅n2\sum_{1\leq i<j<k<\ell\leq n}\alpha_{n}^{(\ell-k)+(j-i)}=(1-o(1))\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{\alpha^{*}}{1-\alpha^{*}}\right)^{2}\cdot n^{2}

.

Proof.

We first find a simpler combinatorial way to count the relevant indices. Let r=ℓ−k≥1r=\ell-k\geq 1, s=j−i≥1s=j-i\geq 1, and t=k−j≥1t=k-j\geq 1. This gives a natural bijection from the indices 1≤i<j<k<ℓ≤n1\leq i<j<k<\ell\leq n to the set of indices 1≤i,s,r,t≤n1\leq i,s,r,t\leq n satisfying i+s+r+t≤ni+s+r+t\leq n. Moreover, for any fixed s,r,ts,r,t satisfying s+r+t≤n−1s+r+t\leq n-1, there are exactly n−r−s−tn-r-s-t valid choices for ii that can admit these gaps. In particular, we may write

∑1≤i<j<k<ℓ≤nα(ℓ−k)+(j−i)\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i<j<k<\ell\leq n}\alpha^{(\ell-k)+(j-i)} =∑i,s,t,r:i+s+t+r≤nαs+r\displaystyle=\sum_{i,s,t,r\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}i+s+t+r\leq n}\alpha^{s+r}

∑u,t:2≤u≤n−2,t+u≤n−1(u−1)αu(n−u−t)\displaystyle\sum_{u,t\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}2\leq u\leq n-2,t+u\leq n-1}(u-1)\alpha^{u}(n-u-t) =∑2≤u≤n−2(u−1)​αu​(∑t=1n−u−1(n−u−t))\displaystyle=\sum_{2\leq u\leq n-2}(u-1)\alpha^{u}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{n-u-1}(n-u-t)\right)
=∑2≤u≤n−2(u−1)​αu​(n−u)​(n−u−1)2.\displaystyle=\sum_{2\leq u\leq n-2}(u-1)\alpha^{u}\frac{(n-u)(n-u-1)}{2}.

At this point, we can expand in nn to find that

∑1≤i<j<k<ℓ≤nα(ℓ−k)+(j−i)=n22​∑u=2n−2(u−1)​αu+O⁡(n),\sum_{1\leq i<j<k<\ell\leq n}\alpha^{(\ell-k)+(j-i)}=\frac{n^{2}}{2}\sum_{u=2}^{n-2}(u-1)\alpha^{u}+O(n),

where we may use standard geometric bounds for the lower order contributions in nn. For this dominant geometric term, we can again apply dominated convergence in the same way as before to find that
